Incident Reporting and Escalation Guide

Purpose
This guide explains how employees must identify, report, and escalate compliance, privacy, security, and operational control incidents. Early reporting helps the company contain impact, preserve evidence, meet legal obligations, and protect customers, employees, and business partners.

What Must Be Reported
Reportable incidents include suspected personal data exposure, unauthorized system access, phishing success, lost or stolen devices containing company information, payment workflow anomalies, policy violations involving customer records, safety events at company-managed sites, and control breakdowns that could create legal or financial risk. Employees should report concerns even when facts are incomplete. Uncertainty is not a reason to wait.

Immediate Actions for Employees
If an employee becomes aware of a potential incident, the employee must first stop any unsafe or harmful activity that can be safely interrupted. Next, preserve relevant evidence such as screenshots, emails, timestamps, order IDs, user accounts, or device details. Then report the issue immediately through the designated incident channel, help desk, or compliance hotline depending on the nature of the event. Employees must not delete evidence, contact external parties without approval, or attempt technical remediation beyond their role authority.

Manager Responsibilities
Managers who receive an incident report must acknowledge receipt promptly, ensure the employee knows the issue has been escalated, and avoid informal side handling outside approved channels. Managers should help gather context, identify impacted customers or operations, and preserve business continuity while the proper response team takes ownership. They must not suppress reporting, delay escalation for reputational reasons, or promise confidentiality beyond approved process limits.

Triage and Severity
The receiving function, typically IT Security, Compliance, or Operations leadership, assigns an initial severity based on data sensitivity, business disruption, number of customers affected, financial exposure, and regulatory implications. High-severity incidents require immediate cross-functional notification and an incident commander. Medium-severity incidents require same-day triage and action planning. Low-severity incidents still require documentation and closure notes.

Documentation Requirements
Every incident record should include the date and time detected, reporter name or channel, affected system or process, summary of observed facts, immediate containment steps, impacted records or transactions if known, and assigned owner. As the investigation progresses, the case file must be updated with decisions, evidence locations, communications issued, and closure approvals.

External Notifications and Legal Review
Only authorized functions may determine whether customers, regulators, carriers, payment partners, or law enforcement need to be notified. Potential privacy incidents involving customer data must be reviewed by Compliance and Legal without delay so statutory notification timelines can be assessed.

Training and Enforcement
All employees complete annual incident reporting training and must follow this guide as a condition of access to company systems and facilities. Deliberate failure to report, concealment of material facts, or unauthorized disclosure during an active incident may result in disciplinary action.

Closure Review
Before an incident is closed, the assigned owner must confirm that containment is complete, required notifications have been evaluated, evidence is retained, and follow-up corrective actions are assigned where needed. Material incidents should receive a documented lessons-learned review.

Management Visibility
High-impact incidents should also be summarized for leadership with clear status, customer impact, current mitigations, and outstanding actions so accountability remains visible until closure.
